segments.text: Ultrasound guided femoral nerve block. The femoral nerve lies lateral to the
femoral artery. The nerve is covered by the fascia iliaca. Of note, the femoral
vessels are enveloped in a separate fascial sheet called the vascular sheet
that may not communicate with the femoral nerve. It is important to note that
multiple fascial sheets can be identified in this region. fasciaolata is one
of them and should not be confused with the fascia iliaca sheet. fasciaolata
appears more superficial and is not anatomically related to the femoral nerve.
The arrows indicate the fascia iliaca. Lateral and superficial to the ilio soas muscle
is a sartoris muscle, which should not be confused with the ilio soas muscle.
We will now spend a few moments discussing the ultrasound anatomy of the femoral nerve block.
The ultrasound transducer is placed over the anterior thigh in the area of the inguinal crease.
The ultrasound image shows the femoral nerve immediately lateral to the femoral artery.
Ultrasound clearly depicts the fascial layers.
The two layers of the fascia iliaca envelop the femoral nerve, which sits on the ilio-sauce
muscle.
The fascia lata is much more superficial, whereas the vascular fascia may not contain the
femoral nerve.
The technique begins with the disinfection of the skin.
A small-gauge needle is used to inject local anaesthetic subcutaneously to decrease the discomfort
during needle manipulation.
In this example, the needle approaches the femoral nerve with an in-plane technique and eventually
enters between the two layers of the fascia iliacca.
Injection of local anaesthetic causes separation of the two layers of the fascia and the distribution
of local anesthetic is clearly seen involving the entire femoral nerve between the two layers of
the fascia. Often times, during the performance of a femoral nerve block, a motor response of
the quadriceps is elicited. If the motor response is present, it is important to ensure that the absence
of the response with a current of less than 0.3 milliamps to decrease the risk of an interfacicular
Injection.
This particular ultrasound anatomy example demonstrates the dispersion of local anesthetic
under the fasciailiaca laterally towards the sartorius muscle.
It is important to note that there are several large vessels in the vicinity of the femoral
nerve.
Therefore, careful aspiration throughout the procedure is crucially important to avoid
an inadvertent, intravascular injection during the block.
